vignette:
Leilani, a 63-year-old project manager of Hawaiian descent, had always prided herself on her ability to keep a dozen moving parts in sync—budgets, timelines, subcontractors, all humming under her quiet, steady hand. That was before the illness. Two years ago, a routine cut on her hand turned into a cascading sepsis that landed her in the intensive care unit for eighteen days. She remembered the blur of fevers and the cold, insistent presence of needles: the arterial line threaded into her wrist, the central line snaking toward her heart, the daily blood draws that left her arm a patchwork of bruises. Most vividly, she remembered the pulmonologist pressing a stethoscope to her chest and saying, “We’re not sure you’re going to make it, Leilani.” She had felt her body surrender, becoming nothing more than a surface upon which machines and hands acted. The shame of that helplessness had settled into her bones alongside the infection.

In the months after discharge, Leilani tried to resume her old life. But she found herself flinching violently when her husband, Mark, touched her shoulder from behind, her heart hammering as though she were back in that bed being prodded without warning. She began to snap at him for the smallest things—leaving a dish in the sink, humming off-key—and then felt a deeper wave of shame for her own irritability. At work, she struggled to hold a thread of concentration through a single project meeting; numbers swam on the whiteboard, and she would catch herself staring at the clock, counting the minutes until she could escape. When a junior team member casually mentioned his father’s colonoscopy during a coffee break, Leilani felt the floor tilt. The word “scope” pressed against her chest like a physical weight. She excused herself, locked herself in the bathroom, and pressed her palm to the cold tile until the wave passed.

The memories came not as words but as sensations. Lying in bed at night, she would suddenly feel her body contort into the same rigid, curled posture she had held in the ICU—knees drawn up, arms crossed over her chest, jaw clenched. The smell of antiseptic would flood her nose, and the phantom pinch of a needle would register in her forearm. She could not describe these episodes to Mark; when she opened her mouth, the only words that came were “I can’t,” and then silence. The event itself had become something that could not be shaped into language, only re-experienced in full color and terror.

Leilani had come to believe that the trauma had hollowed out her life. The woman who had once run marathons and managed $10 million projects now saw her body as a traitorous vessel that could betray her without warning. She felt a deep, private shame about what had happened to her body—the scars, the dependence, the way strangers had seen her naked and inert. She could not trust her own heartbeat: every palpitation felt like the beginning of another collapse. She avoided doctor’s appointments, refused to look at medical equipment in TV shows, and changed the subject whenever anyone mentioned an illness. At her annual performance review, her supervisor noted that she had become “difficult to work with” and that her distraction was affecting deadlines. Leilani knew she was losing grip on the career that had given her identity.

What finally brought her to a therapist’s office was a morning when Mark asked if she wanted to talk about the anniversary of her discharge, and she screamed at him so viciously that he stepped backward into the wall. She saw the hurt in his eyes, and something cracked. She was afraid that she would never feel safe in her own skin again, that the irritability would cost her the marriage she loved, and that the memories would keep returning, unbidden, like a tide she could not outrun. But beneath the fear was a thin thread of hope: that someone might help her find a way to put what had happened into words, and that doing so might loosen the body’s grip on the past.
